 Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas issued a warning about First Amendment protections Monday, after the court declined to hear a challenge to a California requirement governing what instructors must teach doctors in continuing medical education courses. Thomas, joined by fellow conservative Samuel Alito, dissented from the court's refusal to hear Khatibi v. Yip, arguing that a federal appeals court had "fundamentally" misunderstood when speech can be treated as the government's own rather than constitutionally protected private expression. "First Amendment protections do not give way simply because a State heavily regulates speech," Thomas wrote. The decision not to hear the case Monday was not a ruling striking down or upholding California's requirement; instead, it left the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals' judgment in place without deciding the case on the merits. Thomas argued the problem may lie with the Supreme Court's own test for deciding what counts as "government speech" and said the justices should reconsider it. "We are deeply disappointed that the Court declined to take the case," Caleb Trotter, attorney with the Pacific Legal Foundation which brought the case, told Newsweek in a statement. "Now, continuing medical education instructors teaching courses in their private capacity, on their own time, and without any review of their course by the State, have less First Amendment protection than government employees or even public school teachers when speaking in the course of their official duties." Newsweek reached out to the California Attorney General's office for comment Monday morning. What Was Khatibi v. Yip About? California requires licensed doctors to complete 50 hours of approved continuing medical education every two years. The state also requires qualifying courses involving patient care to include instruction concerning implicit bias and its effects on health outcomes, following a law passed in 2019. The courses, Thomas said, could be organized by private entities, accredited by private organizations, and taught by private instructors. The state does not preapprove all course content, although it establishes standards and may audit courses for compliance. Physician Azadeh Khatibi and other challengers argued that forcing instructors to address implicit bias compels private speech in violation of the First Amendment. The case asked a fundamental question: When California tells a private instructor what must be said in a state-required professional course, is the instructor speaking for California or themselves? Why Did Thomas Issue a First Amendment Warning? Normally, the government can express its own views without having to remain unbiased under the First Amendment, but if speech is actually that of a private individual, the government cannot necessarily escape First Amendment scrutiny simply by regulating it or labeling it governmental. Thomas said he believed the Ninth Circuit blurred that distinction by misapplying a previous decision, Shurtleff v. Boston from 2022, in which the Supreme Court found the city of Boston violated the First Amendment when it denied a Christian group's request to fly a Christian flag over City Hall. The court ruled the city's flag-raising program was not government speech and could not, therefore, exclude religious expression. "More fundamentally, however, Shurtleff is leading courts astray," Thomas wrote. The circuit treated the instruction in California's regulated continuing medical education system as government speech. Thomas said that reasoning threatens to create a much broader principle under which sufficiently extensive regulation could effectively turn private expression into government speech. Why Did the Ninth Circuit Reject the First Amendment Challenge? The Ninth Circuit treated the continued training as government speech, rather than ordinary private expression subject to the challengers' compelled-speech theory. The Supreme Court's Shurtleff framework tells courts considering government speech to examine: Thomas said the Ninth Circuit effectively blurred those distinctions by repeatedly relying on the extent of government regulation to determine whether the speech was governmental. "In its blinkered application of the Shurtleff factors, the Ninth Circuit lost sight of the core government-speech inquiry: whether the government is 'speak[ing] for itself or. . . regulat[ing] private expression,'" Thomas wrote. "The government-speech doctrine occupies a narrow corner of our First Amendment jurisprudence. The First Amendment protects the people’s right of free speech against government interference; it does not prevent the government from speaking for itself." This is where the justice traced his concern back to. In 2022, he joined Alito in a separate opinion warning that the court's multi-factor approach might cause lower courts to conclude that heavy government regulation converts private speech into government speech. "There is little in the lower courts' logic to limit that absurd result to medical education," Trotter said. "While this is the end of the road for this important compelled-speech case, we will continue fighting against attempts to require endorsement of government orthodoxy to practice one's profession." What Happens Next The denial means the Supreme Court has not established a new nationwide First Amendment rule in this case, and the Ninth Circuit's decision remains intact, while California's CME regime survives this particular Supreme Court challenge. While this case has been denied, Thomas' viewpoint suggested that another government speech dispute in the future may give him, Alito and, potentially, Neil Gorsuch the opportunity to revisit Shurtleff. "This Court should reconsider whether the Shurtleff test is the proper mode of analysis for identifying government speech," Thomas said.
